title: Redirection and pipes
goal: Send normal output and errors where the user wants them, and connect commands with pipes, tee and xargs.
setup: # P1: a health script that prints OK lines (stdout) and FAIL lines (stderr)
printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' 'echo "OK   nginx is running"' 'echo "FAIL redis is not running" >&2' 'echo "OK   todo-api is running"' 'echo "FAIL postgres port 5432 closed" >&2' > check-services.sh
# P3: image list and temp build files (one name has a space)
# P5: a broken deploy step script

printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/bash' '# Run 3 steps, keep a list of ALL steps in steps.log,' '# save stdout AND stderr of the build in build.log,' '# and restart only if the build worked.' 'build() { echo "compiling todo-api"; echo "error: tests failed" >&2; return 1; }' 'for step in lint test package; do' '  echo "step: $step" > steps.log' 'done' 'build 2>&1 > build.log || echo "restarting service"' > deploy-step.sh

warmup.q: What number do you give `chmod` for a secret file that only the owner may read and write?
What does `usermod -aG docker wicky` do, and why is `-a` important?
warmup.a: It adds wicky to the docker group. Without `-a`, the user is removed from all other extra groups.

warmup.q: Which command shows lines 10 to 12 of a file?
What does `ls -a` show that `ls` does not?
warmup.a: Hidden files: names that start with a dot, like `.env`.

problems.title: Split normal output and errors
problems.situation: A cron job runs `check-services.sh` every 5 minutes. The team wants normal lines in one file and errors in another, and sometimes everything in one log. Each program has two output streams: stdout (normal) and stderr (errors).
task: Run `./check-services.sh`. All 4 lines appear on the screen.
Send only stdout to `ok.log` with `>`. Which lines still appear on the screen?
Send only stderr to `err.log` with `2>`, and hide stdout with `> /dev/null`.
Send both to `all.log` with `> all.log 2>&1`. Then do the same with the short form `&> all2.log`.
Try the wrong order `2>&1 > wrong.log` and look at what goes into the file.
hints: File descriptor 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr. `>` is the same as `1>`.
`2>&1` means "send 2 to the same place as 1 is going **now**". Order matters.
Bash reads redirections from left to right: first `> all.log`, then `2>&1`.
solution: ./check-services.sh > ok.log                  # stdout to file; errors still on screen
./check-services.sh 2> err.log > /dev/null    # only errors to the file, hide the rest
./check-services.sh > all.log 2>&1            # both streams into one file
./check-services.sh &> all2.log               # bash short form of > file 2>&1
./check-services.sh 2>&1 > wrong.log          # WRONG order: errors go to the screen

explanation.meaning: Send stdout (stream 1) to a file. The file is emptied first.
Send stderr (stream 2) to a file.
`/dev/null` is a special file that throws away everything written to it.
First stdout goes to the file, then stderr follows stdout. Both end in the file.
Bash shortcut for `> file 2>&1`.
stderr is pointed to the screen (where stdout was at that moment), then stdout moves to the file. Errors stay on screen.

problems.expected_output:
FAIL redis is not running
FAIL postgres port 5432 closed
--- ok.log ---
OK   nginx is running
OK   todo-api is running
--- err.log ---
FAIL redis is not running
FAIL postgres port 5432 closed
--- all.log ---
OK   nginx is running
FAIL redis is not running
OK   todo-api is running
FAIL postgres port 5432 closed
4 all2.log
FAIL redis is not running
FAIL postgres port 5432 closed
--- wrong.log ---
OK   nginx is running
OK   todo-api is running
mistakes: Writing `2 > err.log` with a space. Bash then passes `2` as an argument and sends stdout to the file.
Using the wrong order `2>&1 > file` in a cron job. Errors are lost, because cron has no screen.
Writing `&2>1`. The correct text is `2>&1` (number, `>`, `&`, number).
problems.interview_say: Every process has stdout (1) and stderr (2). I use `> file 2>&1` to save both, `2> file` for only errors, and `> /dev/null` to hide output. The order matters: the file redirect comes first.
problems.try_yourself: Run `./check-services.sh 2>&1 | grep FAIL`. Then run `./check-services.sh | grep FAIL`. Why is the output the same on the screen but not for the same reason?

problems.title: Overwrite, append and tee: the deploy log
problems.situation: A deploy script writes one line per deploy into `deploy.log`. Yesterday the history disappeared: someone used `>` instead of `>>`. The user also wants to see messages on the screen and save them at the same time.
task: Write `deploy v1.0` and then `deploy v1.1` into `deploy.log`, both with `>`. Show the file.
Add `deploy v1.2` with `>>`. Show the file.
Use `tee -a` to print `health check OK` on the screen **and** add it to the file.
Show the final file with `cat -n deploy.log`.
hints: `>` replaces the file. `>>` adds to the end.
`tee` reads stdin and writes it to the screen and to a file.
`echo "health check OK" | tee -a deploy.log`
solution: echo "deploy v1.1" > deploy.log     # > empties the file first: v1.0 is gone
echo "deploy v1.2" >> deploy.log    # >> adds at the end

explanation.meaning: Create or empty the file, then write.
Append to the end. The old lines stay.
Copy stdin to the screen and append it to the file. Without `-a`, tee replaces the file.
Print with line numbers.

problems.expected_output:
deploy v1.1
health check OK
--- final file ---
     1	deploy v1.1
     2	deploy v1.2
     3	health check OK
mistakes: Using `>` in a loop or a cron job: only the last line is kept.
Writing `tee deploy.log` without `-a`: the log is replaced, like with `>`.
Running `sudo echo x > /etc/file`. The redirect is done by the normal user, so it fails. Use `echo x | sudo tee -a /etc/file` (Extra E2).
problems.interview_say: `>` overwrites and `>>` appends. When I want to see output and save it, I pipe into `tee -a logfile`.
problems.try_yourself: Run `set -o noclobber`, then `echo test > deploy.log`. What happens? Turn it off with `set +o noclobber`.

problems.title: Pipes and xargs: one command for each image
problems.situation: The user must remove old Docker images listed in `images.txt`, and clean temp build files. To be safe, the user first prints the commands with `echo` (a dry run). One temp file has a space in its name.
task: Use `xargs` to build one command with all images: `echo docker rmi ...`.
Use `xargs -n 1` to build one command per image.
Use `xargs -I{}` to build `docker pull registry.local/IMAGE` for each image.
Delete only the `.tmp` files in `tmp-build`, also `c d.tmp`, using `printf '%s\0'` and `xargs -0 rm -v`.
List `tmp-build` to check that `keep.txt` is still there.
hints: `xargs` reads words from stdin and adds them to the end of a command.
`-n 1` = one word per command. `-I{}` = put each line where `{}` is.
Names with spaces break plain xargs. Separate names with a null byte (`\0`) and use `xargs -0`.
solution: xargs echo docker rmi < images.txt                  # one command, all images
xargs -n 1 echo docker rmi < images.txt             # one command per image
xargs -I{} echo docker pull registry.local/{} < images.txt
printf '%s\0' tmp-build/*.tmp | xargs -0 rm -v      # safe with spaces in names

explanation.meaning: Read words from the file and run `cmd` with them as arguments.
Dry run: print the command instead of running it. Remove `echo` when the list is correct.
Use at most 1 argument per command.
Run once per line and replace `{}` with the line.
Separate names with a null byte, so spaces in names are safe.
Verbose: print each file that is removed.

problems.expected_output:
docker rmi todo-frontend:1.4 todo-backend:2.1 postgres:16
docker rmi todo-frontend:1.4
docker rmi todo-backend:2.1
docker rmi postgres:16
docker pull registry.local/todo-frontend:1.4
docker pull registry.local/todo-backend:2.1
docker pull registry.local/postgres:16
removed 'tmp-build/a.tmp'
removed 'tmp-build/b.tmp'
removed 'tmp-build/c d.tmp'
keep.txt
mistakes: `ls tmp-build/*.tmp | xargs rm` splits `c d.tmp` into two names: `rm: cannot remove 'tmp-build/c': No such file or directory`.
Running the real `docker rmi` before checking the list with `echo`.

checks.expect: rm: cannot remove 'tmp-build/c': No such file or directory

problems.interview_say: A pipe sends the output of one command into the input of the next. `xargs` turns input lines into arguments. I always do a dry run with `echo` first, and use `-0` when names can have spaces.
problems.try_yourself: Run `seq 1 6 | xargs -n 2 echo pair:`. Then try `-n 3`.

problems.title: Write a config file with a here-doc
problems.situation: A setup script must create an Nginx config for the to-do app. The port comes from a variable. A here-doc (`<<EOF`) writes many lines into a file in one command, without an editor.
task: Set `APP=todo-api` and `PORT=8080`.
Use `cat > nginx-todo.conf <<EOF ... EOF` to write a small `server { }` block that uses `$PORT` and `$APP`.
Show the file. Check that the real port number is inside.
Print a line with `cat <<'EOF'` (quoted). See that `$APP` is NOT replaced.
Use a here-string `<<<` to split `deploy@web-01` into user and host with `read`.
hints: Unquoted `EOF`: bash replaces variables inside. Quoted `'EOF'`: text stays exactly as written.
The last line must be only `EOF`, with no spaces before or after.
`IFS=@ read -r user host <<< "deploy@web-01"`
solution: Quoted EOF: $APP and $(date) are not replaced

explanation.meaning: Here-doc: all lines until `EOF` become the input of `cat`, which writes them into the file.
With unquoted EOF, variables and `$( )` are replaced.
Quoted: nothing is replaced. Use it for scripts that contain `$`.
Here-string: one string as stdin.
Split the input at `@` into two variables. `IFS` is the field separator.

mistakes: A space after the closing `EOF`, or `EOF` indented: bash does not see the end. It prints a warning with `here-document at line 1 delimited by end-of-file`, and the `EOF ` line goes into the file.
Using unquoted `EOF` for a script that contains `$1` or `$(...)`: they are replaced too early. Use `<<'EOF'`.

checks.expect: here-document at line 1 delimited by end-of-file

problems.interview_say: I use a here-doc to write config files from scripts. Unquoted EOF puts variables in; quoted `'EOF'` keeps the text exactly.
problems.try_yourself: Run `wc -w <<< "one two three"`. Then try `tr a-z A-Z <<< "hello"`.

problems.title: Find the bug: the deploy step script
problems.situation: In Jenkins, `deploy-step.sh` restarted the service even though the build failed. Also `steps.log` has only one line, and the build errors are not in `build.log`. The goal is written in the comments.
task: Read `deploy-step.sh`. Then run `bash deploy-step.sh` and look at `steps.log` and `build.log`.
Find 3 bugs: one is in the loop, one is the redirect order, one is the operator before "restarting".
Fix them. Run the script again and check both files.
hints: Inside the loop, `>` empties `steps.log` every time.
`2>&1 > build.log` sends stderr to the screen. Swap the order.
`||` runs the right side when the left side **fails**. Use `if ... then ... else`.
solution: # Run 3 steps, keep a list of ALL steps in steps.log,
# save stdout AND stderr of the build in build.log,
# and restart only if the build worked.
build() { echo "compiling todo-api"; echo "error: tests failed" >&2; return 1; }
: > steps.log                        # start with an empty file
for step in lint test package; do
if build > build.log 2>&1; then      # file first, then 2>&1

explanation.meaning: Each step emptied the file. Use `>>`, and empty the file once before the loop with `: > steps.log`.
Wrong order, errors went to the screen. Correct: `> build.log 2>&1`.
`a || b` runs `b` when `a` fails. So the service restarted after a failed build. Use `if` (or `&&`).
`:` is a command that does nothing. With `>` it just empties the file.

problems.expected_output:
error: tests failed
restarting service
--- steps.log (before) ---
step: package
build failed: not restarting (see build.log)
--- steps.log ---
step: lint
step: test
step: package
--- build.log ---
compiling todo-api
error: tests failed
mistakes: Writing `build && echo restart || echo failed`. If `echo restart` itself fails, `failed` also prints. An `if` is clearer.
Checking only the screen. With redirects, the useful text is in the file, so always `cat` the log.
problems.interview_say: `&&` runs the next command only on success and `||` only on failure. For a deploy step I use `if build > build.log 2>&1; then restart; fi`, so a failed build never restarts the service.
problems.try_yourself: Change `return 1` to `return 0` in the fixed script and run it. Does it restart now?

problems.title: Group commands: { } vs ( ), and ; && ||
problems.situation: A health report needs several commands in one file, and a script must look into another folder without changing its own folder. The user predicts each line before running.
task: Predict, then run: `{ echo "== report =="; echo "disk ok"; } > report.txt; cat report.txt`.
Predict, then run: `(cd /var/log && pwd); pwd`.
Predict, then run: `X=1; ( X=2 ); echo "X is $X"`.
Predict, then run: `false ; echo A`, `false && echo B`, `false || echo C`.
hints: `{ ...; }` runs in the current shell. Note the spaces and the last `;`.
`( ... )` runs in a subshell (a copy). Changes inside do not come back.
`;` always runs the next command, `&&` only after success, `||` only after failure.
solution: { echo "== report =="; echo "disk ok"; } > report.txt   # one redirect for both
(cd /var/log && pwd)       # subshell: folder change stays inside
false || echo "C: after || because false failed"

explanation.meaning: Group in the current shell. One redirect for all commands.
Subshell. `cd` and variables inside do not change the main shell.
A command that only fails (exit code 1). Good for tests.
always / only if the left side worked / only if the left side failed.

problems.expected_output:
== report ==
disk ok
/var/log
/home/wicky/bash-practice/day04
X is 1
A: after ; always
C: after || because false failed
problems.output_note: `pwd` shows the folder where the user runs it.
mistakes: Writing `{echo a; echo b}` without spaces and the last `;`: bash sees a command called `{echo` and prints `bash: {echo: command not found`.
Expecting a variable set inside `( )` to be available later.
problems.interview_say: Braces group commands in the same shell; parentheses start a subshell, so `cd` and variables inside do not leak out. I use `( cd dir && make )` in scripts to stay in my folder.
problems.try_yourself: Run `( exit 3 ); echo $?`. What exit code do you see?

problems.title: Explain the error: sudo and redirection
problems.situation: A teammate runs `sudo echo "127.0.0.1 todo.local" >> /etc/hosts` and gets `Permission denied`, even with sudo. The user must explain why. Here we test the same idea safely on `/root`, where a normal user cannot write.
task: As your normal user, run `echo hi > /root/note.txt`. Read the error. (It fails, nothing is changed.)
Think: who opens the file in `sudo echo hi > /root/note.txt`? sudo or your shell?
Practise the correct pattern on a copy: copy `/etc/hosts` to `hosts-copy`, then add a line with `echo ... | tee -a hosts-copy > /dev/null`.
Read only: on a real server the fix is `echo "127.0.0.1 todo.local" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts`.
hints: The shell handles `>` before the command starts.
`sudo` gives root rights only to the command after it (`echo`), not to the shell's redirect.
`tee` opens the file itself, so `sudo tee` opens it as root.

explanation.meaning: The user's shell tries to open `/root/note.txt` for writing. The user has no write permission on `/root`.
Same error: `echo` runs as root, but the redirect is still done by the normal shell.
`tee` runs as root and opens the file itself. `-a` appends.
Hide the copy that `tee` prints on the screen.

problems.expected_output:
bash: /root/note.txt: Permission denied
exit code: 1
127.0.0.1 todo.local
mistakes: Using `sudo bash -c 'echo ... >> /etc/hosts'` everywhere. It works, but quoting gets hard. `sudo tee -a` is simpler.
Forgetting `-a` with tee: `sudo tee /etc/hosts` replaces the whole hosts file.
problems.interview_say: The redirect is done by my shell, not by the command, so `sudo echo x > file` still fails. I use `echo x | sudo tee -a file` instead.
problems.try_yourself: Run `ls -ld /root`. Which permission bits explain the error?

interview.q: What is the difference between `>` and `>>`?
interview.a: `>` creates or empties the file and writes. `>>` adds to the end and keeps old content.
Send stderr (2) to the same place as stdout (1) at that moment. `cmd > file 2>&1` puts both in the file.
It is a special file that throws away everything. `cmd > /dev/null 2>&1` hides all output.

interview.q: What is the difference between a pipe `|` and a redirect `>`?
interview.a: A pipe connects the output of one command to the input of another command. A redirect sends output to a file.
It reads stdin and writes it to the screen and to a file at the same time. `tee -a` appends.

recap.meaning: Write (overwrite) / append stdout to a file
Send stdout and stderr to one file
Pipe: output of one command into the next
Show on screen and append to file
Run once per line, {} = the line
Group in this shell / in a subshell
